Product direction

Hibi helps people write notes and documentation in local files and nested folders. Writing should be ready as soon as the app opens. Markdown supports visual, source, and side-by-side editing; other formats offer the views they can support. A workspace can also become a portable documentation site.

Design priorities

Keep writing central and secondary controls quiet.
Share navigation between settings, workspaces, and exported documentation.
Preserve files and unsaved edits through every view change.
Use short, subtle motion to explain changes without repeatedly rewrapping text.
Keep keyboard navigation, labeled controls, rebindable shortcuts, and reduced-motion options. Honor the user's focus-indicator preference.

Use VS Code's file navigation and Codex's sidebar-aware window layout as references. Avoid decorative panels, unnecessary borders, large default gaps, and flickering settings.

Architecture and security

Source layout


: windows, validated IPC, document and workspace access, and native addons.

: the typed bridge. It exposes no general IPC, filesystem, or Node APIs.

Privileged operations

The main process checks the sender, main frame, and exact app URL before every privileged operation. File dialogs grant access to paths. Workspace calls accept only relative document paths within the selected canonical folder. Native addon calls require an enabled addon and an explicitly registered method.

Document replacement, export, and addon preference writes share an operation guard. Closing the app waits for an active operation and checks for unsaved edits. Workspace watchers debounce changes and read asynchronously. New save destinations resolve their parent directory first, so later saves through a symlink compare the same canonical path and still detect external edits.

Local images are bound to the current document revision. The main process resolves relative references from that document's native path, limits reads to 8 MiB, and validates image content before returning a data URL. This bridge cannot read arbitrary files. Documentation snapshots use the same validated images.

Appearance and licenses

Colorschemes contain validated hex colors and attribution. The app and exported site share the same color roles. Appearance IPC accepts a valid preference pair and opaque hex window colors; its cache is written atomically and read before window creation. Exports receive preferences through the workspace snapshot, so the documentation addon does not import core code.

The Hibi settings page reads the bundled license catalog through validated IPC. Lists contain metadata; license text loads when a catalog ID is selected. IDs are looked up in the catalog, never used as paths. The sponsor action opens one fixed HTTPS address and accepts no destination from the renderer.

Runtime boundaries

The renderer is sandboxed and isolated, with Node integration disabled. App assets use a local protocol that rejects path traversal. External navigation, child windows, downloads, and permissions are denied. Development connects only to its local Vite server.

Static exports escape embedded JSON, sanitize rendered Markdown with DOMPurify, and allow only the application script identified by its hash. Fonts and CSS are bundled. Addon code is trusted at build time; opening a workspace never loads its JavaScript as addon code.

CodSpeed

Both native runners use

Each task has one warmup round and five measured rounds. Fresh profiles are unique; retained-profile rounds reuse the warmed profile. Typing, document-open, and source-switch tasks prepare a fresh ready app before timing the action. CodSpeed covers only core and default-enabled addons. Optional-addon profiles, minimal Electron, macOS reopen, extra typing samples, and bundle reports remain in the local diagnostic script.

The workflow builds the current revision, runs Electron under Xvfb on Ubuntu, and authenticates with OIDC. [Walltime] works on hosted runners, with scheduling variance. Finding startup work

Renderer

Native startup rules

The 
 scheme allows V8 code caching.
Native addon implementations load on their first authorized call. Share in-flight imports and recheck enabled state after loading. Resolve worker entrypoints from the application root, independent of chunk splitting.
Installed macOS apps use their bundle icon. Development sets one 256 px Dock icon. Windows/Linux retain window icons.
Load archive download/extraction dependencies only when installing an addon.
Read independent preferences concurrently. Appearance, protocol security, permissions, and IPC must be ready before navigation. Other reads can overlap renderer loading, but IPC must await them before using session state or editing.
Read recent workspaces with initial document metadata and addon preferences. Reapplying unchanged interface casing must not rewrite preferences or rebuild menus.

Renderer startup rules

Catalogs import data-only manifests and lightweight 
 descriptors. Keep detection separate from nodes, renderers, fonts, and export code, so disabled syntax remains detectable without its engine. Load implementations only when enabled. Keep

Wait for the initial document name before selecting required formats. An unknown name must not put every enabled format engine on the startup path. Required schema, serialization, matching formats, and input addons must finish 
 before editing becomes available. A failed required addon leaves source-only editing available. Older API v1 addons retain this conservative behavior.

Use 
 only for services/UI that cannot change editing semantics, such as keyboard sounds. Unrelated enabled formats and background services activate at idle after required capabilities. Disabling an addon during activation invalidates its registrations. Keep existing editors mounted and inert during required capability changes.

Code-language metadata stays available at startup. Cache parser loads and update highlighting without changing source or undo history. An import finishing after disable must not re-enable a language. Async Markdown exports await requested parsers; synchronous API v1 exports may initially contain escaped plain code.

Settings and history load on interaction. Keep the small command palette in the shell bundle: its former lazy fallback resized the editor before the modal opened, causing first-open stutter. Palette search loads settings discovery on demand rather than duplicating setting metadata. Settings stay mounted after first use to retain navigation, while casing initializes independently.

Source-editor modules may warm at idle, but mount the editor only when a source view is requested. Fonts, layout, and asynchronous input extensions must finish before reporting readiness. Failed input extensions show an error and leave source read-only until they load or are disabled.

Focus the initial rich editor synchronously on mount. Never schedule a later selection reset that can overwrite a user's selection.

These results describe the revisions named below. They are historical comparisons, not measurements of the current release. See [performance measurement] to repeat them.

Input and workspace readiness

The benchmark starts before Electron launches and waits for editable text and three populated, enabled recent-workspace buttons. The tested revision is 
. Each profile has six fresh launches and five retained-profile launches after one excluded priming launch. Tests used the same macOS arm64 machine, Electron 44.3.0, production assets, isolated profiles, hidden windows, and automation as the earlier comparison below. These are not installed-app or OS cold-cache timings.

Milliseconds, **median / p95**:

Profile | Before | After |
--- | ---: | ---: |
Default addons, fresh profile | 542.2 / 563.2 | 481.1 / 499.4 |
Default addons, retained profile | 544.8 / 554.9 | 437.9 / 473.1 |
Enabled addon mix, fresh profile | 645.3 / 686.4 | 507.4 / 533.1 |
Enabled addon mix, retained profile | 647.5 / 650.7 | 473.1 / 501.7 |

With default addons, median 
 improved from 456.0 to 404.3 ms for fresh profiles and from 465.2 to 362.4 ms for retained profiles. This records the first painted window while the harness keeps it hidden, separately from input/list readiness.

The default baseline is

With these small samples, p95 is the slowest observed launch. **500ms is not a guaranteed budget:** the final default profile met it locally, but the enabled profile still exceeded it on fresh launches and at the retained-profile tail. Earlier repeated runs also had larger outliers.

The changes reduced these measured costs:

Setting the full-size macOS dock icon cost about 67–71ms per call in an isolated probe. Installed apps now use their bundle icon; development uses a 256px dock icon and omits redundant macOS window-icon assignment.
Addon archive dependencies no longer load on launch. The main entry fell from 561,033 to 194,401 bytes at that change.
A CPU profile attributed about 122ms to keybeats' cold 
 creation. Asynchronous device discovery moved service preparation off the editor thread's critical path; an isolated follow-up constructor probe took about 4ms. Discovery itself took about 858ms asynchronously. Sounds can arrive after editing is ready; typing does not wait for them.
The recent-workspace read now overlaps initial document and addon loading. Unchanged interface casing no longer rewrites preferences or reconstructs the menu.
Format activation waits for the document name before choosing required engines. Keyboard sounds start in the existing background lane. Required Markdown schemas, serializers, and input features remain gated.

First-displayed-keystroke p95 was 24.7 ms fresh / 23.5 ms retained with default addons, and 40.1 ms / 27.0 ms with the enabled mix. Startup readiness covers recent-workspace choices, not opening and indexing a large workspace. Windows/Linux, signed installed-app launch, OS cold-cache behavior, and other audio device configurations were not measured.

Lookup and bounds

The lookup worker keeps sorted spelling keys and compact 32-bit reference arrays in an LRU cache with a 256 MiB accounting cap. Typed arrays are charged their exact byte lengths; strings and their array slots receive a conservative UTF-16 allowance with object overhead. This cap describes retained index data, not total process RSS or temporary parsing allocations. The worker validates the existing sorted JSON index format and converts it to these arrays once, preserving compatibility with installed packs. Exact and normalized lookups use binary search. The worker returns bounded entry records; the renderer receives no paths. Converter headwords and aliases, lookup queries, and completion prefixes use Unicode NFC normalization. Exact keys win before case-normalized keys. A full French source audit on 12 October 2026 found all 400,911 existing index keys already in NFC, so its installed format remains compatible without rebuilding. English also uses the WordNet XML's 4,473 explicit inflected forms, including irregular forms such as 
, 
, and

The worker has a 512 MiB old-generation heap limit. Conversion caps are one million entries, 750,000 keys, 1.5 million references, 512 MiB of entry data, and 48 MiB of index data. Each packed record is at most 64 KiB. Source decompression is capped at 512 MiB, except French's 768 MiB and German's 1.5 GiB; source records are capped at 2 MiB. The runtime admits at most 64 queued jobs. Each lookup returns at most 32 records and 512 KiB. Directory/file checks reject symlinks; the loader validates ordering, offsets, record boundaries, and key membership.

After the addon starts, an asynchronous native query schedules one preload at a time on idle main-process turns for its preferred Latin and Han languages plus the last successfully used offline pack, when installed. All other packs load lazily. Index parsing and loading happen in the lookup worker; startup does not wait for them. Preload shares checksum verification with foreground queries. A lookup arriving before preload finishes can still pay the cold-load cost. The installed-language list is cached in main and invalidated when installation, cancellation, failure, or removal changes pack state; provider availability queries return a cached boolean instead of listing every pack.

Analysis isolation

The analysis service runs addon analysis in a worker inside a hidden sandboxed renderer process. Each addon uses a separate in-memory session and each process gets a new origin. The main application renderer retains its own sandbox and context isolation settings. Electron documents the underlying boundaries in [Process Sandboxing] and [protocol sessions].

The session serves only its trusted host, worker wrapper, and approved addon module. Content Security Policy and request filtering deny network traffic, frames, and unrelated resources. The addon runs in the worker, where neither DOM access nor either preload bridge exists. The host bridge accepts one bounded JSON completion for the current request. Native handlers bind it to the service's sender, frame, origin, addon, and request ID; payload fields cannot select another owner or document.

Before granting a projection, the main process checks the active tab, revision, content version, and each literal source span. It strips extra fields and checks the document identity again when work completes. Results never modify documents directly. The renderer must still validate their shape and use the normal versioned edit API.

Cancellation destroys the process and settles active and queued requests. The service limits queue depth, output size, process count, request duration, and sampled working-set memory. These limits keep ordinary runaway work away from typing; they do not replace Chromium's sandbox or provide a hard operating-system memory quota. The integration tests cover denied capabilities, owner spoofing, stale documents, queue replacement, oversized output, infinite loops, crash recovery, disable, and reload.
Document-engine migration

The document-engine work preserves each format's original source while replacing whole-document work in editing paths. Source editing, visual authoring, preview and final compiler layout are separate capabilities. A preview or a raw-source dialog does not establish visual editing support.

Persistent source foundation


 implements an internal persistent piece B+ tree. Published snapshots own immutable nodes and chunk ranges. A local replacement copies affected paths and bounded descriptor arrays; untouched chunks and subtrees remain shared. Splits and joins restore node occupancy, including after bulk deletion. The initial experimental defaults are 32 children per branch, 64 pieces per leaf and 4,096 UTF-16 units per original chunk. These are candidates pending integrated editor measurements, not established optimal constants.

Each chunk has private sparse coordinate indexes. Subtree summaries combine raw UTF-16 length, normalized length, UTF-8 size and logical newline count, including CRLF and surrogate pairs crossing piece boundaries. Raw positions inside CRLF are not normalized editor positions. Exact edits also reject split surrogate pairs. Streaming encoding carries a pending high surrogate across chunks. This describes encoding of the source string; it does not introduce a new policy for decoding invalid file bytes.


 contains one document identity, base/result versions, operation identity, origin, history group and sorted disjoint raw changes. The store validates all changes before publication. Preparation returns a private capability; forged, consumed, aborted or stale preparations cannot commit. Inverse edits use post-state coordinates and expand only where necessary to restore a newly formed CRLF or Unicode seam. Undo is a new operation with a higher content version.

Snapshots remain readable after edits and compaction. Compaction changes the storage epoch without changing the content version. JavaScript reachability currently retains chunks needed by snapshots; session-level history, job ownership, journal and save integration must provide the corresponding retention bounds. Mutable hot gaps and transferable shared backing buffers are not used.

Insertions share a private append-only arena. Each published piece freezes its readable range; later writes only extend the allocation beyond that range. Sparse prefix entries below an existing extent never change. Consecutive ranges in source order coalesce into one piece, while separate cursors may share storage without sharing an occurrence. Aborted preparations can leave unused slots. The writer retains at most one chunk; gaps in chunks still referenced by live pieces require compaction. Compaction seals the current writer. Arena typed arrays and writer handles never leave the kernel. Counters distinguish allocated and written arena units, and benchmarks include external/ArrayBuffer memory as well as JavaScript heap use.

Recovery admission and checkpoints

Source and rich edits use one preload journal. Before committing source, history or the editor view, the session checks journal capacity. Saturation rejects that attempted edit with a notice; previously accepted edits stay intact. Save retries recovery, and editing can resume when capacity is available. The normal admission budget is 8 MiB of estimated retained UTF-16 payload and range overhead, including outstanding transport calls. An empty journal allows one bulk message up to 40 MiB; its transport can retain a second copy. These are conservative accounting limits, not measurements of Electron wire traffic or total process memory. Native document-size validation still applies independently.

Delivery has a five-second deadline and three background retries, after 100 ms, 500 ms and two seconds. Manual save/close barriers can retry after that budget. A timeout cannot cancel Electron IPC: an outstanding transport is reused until it settles, and its bytes remain accounted even after a verified checkpoint retires the queue entry. Recovery controls likewise permit only one outstanding request. Thus repeated retries cannot accumulate abandoned full checkpoint or operation payloads.

Native duplicate receipts retain at most 128 operations and 8 MiB of estimated payload. A barrier that cannot recover through ordinary retries pauses new sends, captures the renderer's current checkpoint, reads the native head and replays the exact contiguous pending suffix. Native verification compares complete source, identity and version in bounded chunks, yielding between work slices and rejecting a changed text generation or foreign store. An owned storage-only replacement remains valid. Only a matching checkpoint retires older pending entries whose receipts expired. Edits accepted during verification wait in the same queue and are delivered afterward. The checkpoint is read-only: it cannot overwrite different native content or conceal a missing operation.

The internal recovery-state API distinguishes queued payloads, outstanding transport payloads, failed/retrying delivery and the latest memory acknowledgement. The session owns the local version; normal document state owns the file-saved baseline. A memory acknowledgement provides renderer-crash recovery, **not** a disk-durable acknowledgement. Loss of the replica's source beyond the available operation suffix remains a recoverable error; this protocol does not claim whole-app crash recovery or authorize an unverified bootstrap overwrite.

Document persistence

The renderer sends text changes to the main process through one ordered journal. It accepts legacy UTF-16 replacements and atomic 
 batches. Both include the tab, document revision, previous content version and next content version. Atomic batches also carry an operation ID, origin and history group. All ranges use the same pre-state. The main process validates the entire operation and size limit before committing it, then acknowledges that version. It rejects stale documents, missing changes, conflicting retries and invalid Unicode boundaries.

Each tab has a persistent source store and an immutable saved snapshot. Accepted changes update that store without reconstructing the complete source string. Tab metadata and ordinary dirty checks do not materialize document text. Full source remains available for explicit legacy reads, saving and export. A bounded receipt cache makes recent retries idempotent; a lost acknowledgment does not apply the edit twice. Atomic acknowledgments include the operation ID. Preload retains unacknowledged changes, accounts for their queued bytes, and retries them in order at a flush barrier. A failed barrier rejects the dependent action instead of saving an older snapshot.

Desktop requests that read or act on document content pass through this barrier, including save, autosave, export, tab changes, and addon operations. Native window close also requests a barrier before checking unsaved documents. The legacy whole-source update method remains available and waits for earlier changes.

Preload announces journal readiness before exposing editing APIs. Closing a window before that bridge exists does not wait for a response it cannot send; existing native snapshots still receive the unsaved-change check.

The main-process snapshot survives a renderer crash. It is not a disk journal: a whole-app crash or power loss can still lose unsaved work. Autosave and ordinary saving provide disk persistence, including the existing checks for external file changes.

The recovery screen can reload the main frame's trusted app entrypoint and recover the native snapshot. The navigation guard allows that same entrypoint in production and development while rejecting other paths, query strings, external destinations and subframe navigation. A failed editor-module load uses this same recovery path.

Saving captures a particular immutable source snapshot. Completing that write updates the saved baseline for that snapshot, while newer source remains dirty. Exact source operations reject boundaries inside CRLF. The legacy bridge preserves its previous raw-offset meaning by extending only a split CRLF boundary before applying it to the store.

Renderer migration to exact operation production is ongoing; legacy producers may still flatten and diff source before enqueueing. Receipt-horizon resynchronization and sender backpressure remain separate migration work. See the [document-engine migration] for the distinction between implemented foundations and complete editor integration.

Privacy boundary

Records use a finite event catalog, integer locations, static roles and reasons, and a small error-code allowlist. No generic object serializer, arbitrary metadata bag, console interception or raw exception message is supported. Renderer records cross a separate raw IPC channel in bounded batches. Main validates frame ownership, origin, generation, fields, sizes and artifact IDs again. A transport acknowledgement means the batch was consumed, including deliberate drops; it does not promise disk persistence or document recovery.

Admission happens before stack projection. Native error branding and own data descriptors allow already materialized original stacks without invoking getters or

Unknown headers or prototypes, lazy stack accessors and arbitrary thrown objects are omitted. Neither names nor messages enter the result. Browser-owned error coordinates can provide an original frame. Stack text is bounded before parsing, and only exact trusted artifact locations survive. Eval frames, unknown sourceURL labels, query-bearing URLs and unknown locations are omitted. The catalog constrains output; it cannot authenticate a deliberately forged stack from already compromised application code. A caller-created stack is not evidence of the original failure and must never be substituted.

Autocomplete

Enable **Autocomplete** in **Settings → Addons**. It requires **Dictionary and thesaurus**. Installed offline dictionary packs supply suggestions before anything has been learned; autocomplete never downloads packs or sends network requests. Dictionary lookups and pack installation remain separate actions in the dictionary addon.

Type at least three Latin letters to see word suggestions. After a space, the preceding one or two words can suggest the next word when repeated use gives one choice a clear lead. Repeatedly writing “bro that was wild” can suggest “wild” after “that was”; unrelated contexts show nothing. English, French, German, and Filipino can be used together. Choose at least one language in Autocomplete settings. Chinese and Japanese word segmentation is not supported yet.

Suggestions start with no word selected. While typing a word, use the arrow keys to highlight a completion and Enter to accept it. **Accept suggestions with Tab** is on by default: Tab accepts the highlighted in-word completion, or the first one when none is highlighted. Turn it off to leave Tab to the editor while suggestions are visible. For next-word suggestions after a space, arrow keys dismiss the list and move the caret; Enter and Tab keep their normal editor behavior. Click a next-word suggestion to accept it. Escape dismisses the list. Accepting a suggestion makes one undo step. The dictionary's previous suggestion, language, and Tab preferences move to Autocomplete at startup. If dictionary suggestions were on, Autocomplete is enabled unless you explicitly disabled it.

Learning and privacy

Autocomplete learns from words committed while typing, not from opening documents or pasting text. Accepted words receive a small boost. Undoing or overwriting an accepted suggestion within ten seconds reduces its influence; ignoring a suggestion does not count against it. Repeated observations matter more than one unusual word. Spelling preferences come from words used within sentences, so sentence-start capitals do not turn ordinary completions into names. Completions follow the case you type; internal capitals such as “iPhone” and “McDonald” are preserved. Slang and mixed-language patterns are supported. Older observations gradually lose influence, with a thirty-day half-life.

Learning and ranking happen on this device. Each Hibi profile keeps separate data. Workspaces keep separate histories, and documents outside workspaces share their own history. Workspace words are never used as a global fallback. Dictionary custom words remain available as vocabulary independently of learning.

Stored data contains individual words, counts, correction counts, timestamps, language membership, and at most two preceding words per entry. It does not contain complete sentences, documents, or a keystroke log. Up to 4,096 aggregate entries across sixteen recent scopes are kept; old or weak entries are pruned. Data lives in Hibi's addon storage inside your profile, outside workspace folders.

Code blocks, inline code, frontmatter, link URLs, math, raw HTML, and secret-looking text are excluded. These checks are conservative, not a way to recognize every secret. Use **Exclude this document** or **Exclude this workspace** for private writing. Exclusions stop learning and personal suggestions there; they do not erase words already learned. Clear the relevant history to remove existing data.

Turn off **Learn from my writing** to pause learning and personal ranking. Offline dictionary suggestions still work. Excluding a document or workspace discards its queued observations. Turning learning off discards all queued observations and keeps existing counts for later. Other settings changes save queued observations.

Clear learned words

Choose **Clear learned words** in Autocomplete settings, select **This workspace** or **Everything**, and confirm. Outside a workspace, the first choice clears the shared history for documents outside workspaces. **Everything** clears both workspace histories and that shared history. You can also run **Autocomplete: clear learned words** from the command palette.

Clearing removes the selected counts from memory and writes the cleared data to disk immediately, including histories for workspaces that are not open. The success notice appears after the disk write completes. Dictionary packs and custom dictionary words are kept. New typing can begin learning again while learning is enabled.

Current limits

Suggestions use the existing completion list in both editors. The formatted editor currently inserts completions in top-level paragraphs and headings. Source view conservatively checks the first 16,384 characters for safe prose; later text does not contribute to autocomplete until that syntax proof can be maintained incrementally. Very long formatted textblocks have the same proof limit. Suggestions may be absent around unsupported or incomplete syntax.

The starting dictionary ranking favors exact accent matches and single words, then languages in the order you enabled them and shorter words. Lowercase headwords rank ahead of names unless you type a capital; German nouns keep their normal capitalization. Packs supply a limited prefix list without frequency information, so the most common word is not always present. Personal ranking improves with repeated use; it does not attempt sentence generation.
